candidate.blueprint_topic: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control — safe access of an implanted central venous port
candidate.educational_objective: Apply evidence-based implanted-port access steps, including pre-access assessment, skin antisepsis, and use of a non-coring needle without overstating a universal sterile-glove requirement.

options.A: Perform hand hygiene, inspect and cleanse the port site with an appropriate antiseptic, and access the septum with a non-coring needle.
options.B: Use a standard hypodermic needle because any sterile needle can safely penetrate the port septum.
options.C: Omit skin antisepsis when the port has been accessed recently and the skin appears clean.
options.D: Access the port before inspecting the surrounding chest and neck so manipulation does not alter the assessment findings.

candidate.rationale: CDC outpatient oncology guidance for implanted ports directs the nurse to perform hand hygiene, examine the site and surrounding chest/neck for complications, cleanse the port site with an appropriate antiseptic, stabilize the portal body, and insert a non-coring needle such as a Huber needle until the portal backing is felt. CDC notes that clean or sterile gloves may be used for implanted-port access and that professional-society recommendations differ, so the final item does not incorrectly require one universal glove type. A standard hypodermic needle, skipped antisepsis, or access before site assessment is not consistent with the described procedure.
candidate.source_claim_supported: CDC's implanted-port access procedure includes hand hygiene, examination of the site and veins of the chest and neck, clean or sterile gloves, cleansing with an appropriate antiseptic, stabilization of the portal body, and insertion of a non-coring needle such as a Huber needle.
